run.question: Debug memory issues for my Python application orca in namespace app-95

report.summary: Fetched runbook python-memory-troubleshooting and carried out its steps with my own tools: (1) application status - Deployment orca in app-95 has 1/1 ready, single pod orca-57fdcbf45f-q9jgw on node opspilot-m1-control-plane; (2) logs - the container's own log shows a monotonically growing retained-image footprint (24.0 MB at 20 images, 63.0 MB at 50, 97.8 MB at 80, 120.6 MB at 100) and the configuration lines 'Storing all processed images for audit trail' and 'Caching thumbnails for quick retrieval'; (3) code patterns - cache/processed_images counters grow with each image and never shrink in the logs, but the application source is mounted from Secret orca-app, which cannot be read, so I could not inspect for eviction logic; (4) memory growth - growth is essentially linear (~1.2 MB per processed image); (5) memory metrics/limits - kubectl-top equivalent and Prometheus were unavailable (SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE on every Prometheus call), so growth is quantified from the application's own log lines, and the effective limit from the Deployment spec is 128Mi memory / 64Mi request. Observed outcome: the container was OOMKilled with exit code 137 twice - finished 09:19:28 and again 09:19:58 - after each ~30 s run in which it processed ~100 images and reported ~120.6 MB of stored images, and the pod is now Ready=False (ContainersNotReady). Node-level memory pressure is not present (MemoryPressure=False, 32859944Ki allocatable) and there is no Evicted event, so the kills are cgroup memory-limit kills of this container, not node pressure. The supported cause is therefore the Deployment app-95/orca's 128Mi memory limit being too small for the application's retain-everything design; the unreadable application code is the likely deeper contributor but remains a hypothesis. Prometheus and change_history were not available, so memory time series and whether the limit was recently changed could not be verified.

claims.text: Container 'orca' of pod orca-57fdcbf45f-q9jgw in namespace app-95 has lastState terminated with reason OOMKilled and exitCode 137, finishedAt 2026-11-22T09:19:28Z, restartCount 1; the pod started at 09:18:56Z and has memory limit 128Mi and requests cpu 10m / memory 64Mi.

The same container was OOMKilled a second time: state.terminated reason OOMKilled, exitCode 137, startedAt 2026-11-22T09:19:29Z, finishedAt 2026-11-22T09:19:58Z, while the pod's Ready and ContainersReady conditions became False with reason ContainersNotReady at 09:19:59Z.

Deployment orca in namespace app-95 runs 1 replica of image python:3.9-slim with command ['python','/app/app.py'], env PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 and SERVICE_NAME=orca-image-processor, resources limits {memory: 128Mi} and requests {cpu: 10m, memory: 64Mi}, and mounts /app from secret 'orca-app'; the Deployment's reported ready and available replica counts are 1.

The dead container instance's log shows retained-image memory rising with every batch and no eviction: 'Approximate memory used by stored images' 24.0 MB at 20 images (09:18:59), 63.0 MB at 50 (09:19:02), 97.8 MB at 80 (09:19:17), 120.6 MB at 100 images (09:19:27), immediately followed by 'Processing image 101' at 09:19:28 and the OOMKill, with 'Cache size: N thumbnails' and 'Memory usage: processed_images list has N items' growing in lockstep.

The restarted container logs the configuration it is running with - 'Configuration: Storing all processed images for audit trail' and 'Configuration: Caching thumbnails for quick retrieval' - and repeats the same growth pattern (11.2 MB at 10 images to 62.3 MB at 50 images within five seconds of start), i.e. the accumulation is the application's designed behavior, not a one-off.

The only ConfigMap in namespace app-95 is kube-root-ca.crt, so no orca ConfigMap holds these settings; the settings shown in the logs are not backed by a ConfigMap in that namespace (the code comes from Secret orca-app, which cannot be read).

ReplicaSet orca-57fdcbf45f owned by Deployment orca was created at 2026-11-22T09:18:56Z with deployment.kubernetes.io/revision 1 and the same 128Mi limit; it is the only ReplicaSet in app-95, and the window's events are only Normal ones (Deployment ScalingReplicaSet, ReplicaSet SuccessfulCreate, Pod Scheduled/Pulled/Created/Started), with no Evicted, OOMKilling, SystemOOM or FailedScheduling event.

Node opspilot-m1-control-plane, where the pod runs, reports MemoryPressure False with reason KubeletHasSufficientMemory and 32859944Ki allocatable memory, so the kills are not caused by node-level memory pressure.
The 128Mi limit seen in the Deployment spec of app-95/orca is the only orca memory limit in the cluster; no other Deployment matching 'orca' exists in any namespace.

The container's 128Mi memory limit is below the steady-state footprint of this workload (~1.2 MB retained per processed image, so ~100 images already exceed the limit): the app is killed before it can run indefinitely, and it will keep being OOMKilled every ~30 s cycle unless the limit is raised or the retained data is bounded.

The deeper cause is in the application code mounted from Secret orca-app: the logs show 'processed_images' and a thumbnail cache that only grow ('Cache size: N thumbnails', 'processed_images list has N items') with the enabled 'Storing all processed images for audit trail' / 'Caching thumbnails for quick retrieval' behavior, consistent with an unbounded cache/list without eviction; the source could not be read to confirm.

The Deployment and pod look superficially healthy: Deployment orca reports 1 ready and 1 available replica and the pod phase is Running with Ready briefly true after each restart at 09:19:29Z, while its container had already been OOMKilled once and was OOMKilled again at 09:19:58Z - so ready/available replica counts do not show the memory failure.

Node memory pressure or node-level OOM killing the container: the node reports MemoryPressure False (KubeletHasSufficientMemory, 32859944Ki allocatable) and no SystemOOM/Evicted event exists, while the container itself carries OOMKilled with exit code 137.

A pod-template change or rollout left the workload broken: the only ReplicaSet (orca-57fdcbf45f) is revision 1, created together with the pod at 09:18:56Z and still the current ReplicaSet, so the restarts are same-template container restarts (OOMKilled), not a config-triggered rollout.

Raise the container memory limit (and matching request) of Deployment app-95/orca above the workload's steady-state footprint instead of 128Mi, sized from measured RSS under the real image rate rather than the ~1.2 MB/image log estimate alone.

Bound the retained data in the application (size-limited/evicting thumbnail cache and a capped or persisted audit trail for processed_images), since the logs show both structures only grow; add a memory-exporter or /metrics and repeat runs after the change to confirm the footprint plateaus.

gaps: Prometheus was unreachable for this Run (get_metric_names and execute_prometheus_instant_query returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE), so container memory series such as container_memory_working_set_bytes, restart/error-rate series and a pre-incident memory baseline could not be read; memory growth is quantified only from the application's own log lines.
The application source is mounted from Secret orca-app and secrets cannot be read, so the unbounded-cache/processed_images code path could not be verified and remains a hypothesis.

No LimitRange was checkable (kind not available in the tool's resource list) and change_history is not integrated, so where the 128Mi limit came from and whether it was changed shortly before the incident are unknown.

Pod state after 2026-11-22T09:19:35Z (end of the authorized window) is only partially visible: fetch_pod_logs dropped 19 lines after the window end, though pod status at 09:20:03Z showed the second OOMKill.
Jaeger's service list does not include orca, so no trace data exists for this workload; traces were not queried for it.
Impact beyond this single replica (e.g. consumers of the image-processing output) was not observed; nothing in the evidence shows downstream or customer impact.
